title: Part 1, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Raskolnikov was not used to crowds, and as mentioned before, he had been avoiding all human contact, especially lately. But now he suddenly felt a desire to be around other people. Something new seemed to be stirring inside him, and with it came a kind of thirst for company. He was so exhausted after a solid month of concentrated misery and dark agitation that he wanted to escape, if only for a moment, into some other world, any world at all. And despite the filthy surroundings, he was glad to stay in the tavern.

The owner was in another room but kept coming down a few steps into the main area, his flashy tarred boots with red turned-down tops appearing before the rest of him. He wore a long coat and a hideously greasy black satin waistcoat with no tie, and his entire face seemed smeared with oil like a door lock. A boy of about fourteen stood behind the counter, and a younger boy handed out whatever was ordered. On the counter lay sliced cucumber, pieces of dried black bread, and chopped-up fish, all reeking. The air was suffocating, so thick with the fumes of alcohol that five minutes in there could make a person drunk.

Sometimes you meet a stranger who captures your interest from the very first moment, before a single word is spoken. That was the impression made on Raskolnikov by a man sitting a short distance away who looked like a retired clerk. The young man would recall this impression many times afterward, and even attributed it to some kind of premonition. He kept glancing at the clerk, partly because the man was staring persistently at him, clearly eager to start a conversation. The clerk looked at everyone else in the room, including the tavern keeper, as if he were bored with their company and felt a condescending contempt for people beneath his station and education -- people not worth talking to. He was a man past fifty, bald and graying, medium height, heavily built. His face, bloated from constant drinking, had a yellowish, almost greenish tinge, with puffy eyelids from which sharp reddish eyes peered out like narrow slits. But there was something very strange about him -- a light in his eyes suggesting intense feeling, perhaps even thought and intelligence, but also a glint of something like madness. He wore an old and hopelessly tattered black dress coat with every button missing except one, which he kept fastened, clearly clinging to this last shred of respectability. A crumpled shirt front, spotted and stained, stuck out from his canvas waistcoat. Like a proper clerk, he was clean-shaven, but it had been so long since he last shaved that his chin looked like a stiff grayish brush. There was still something respectable, something official, about his manner. But he was restless -- he kept running his fingers through his hair and from time to time would let his head sink into his hands, his tattered elbows resting wearily on the stained, sticky table. Finally he looked straight at Raskolnikov and said loudly and firmly:

"May I venture, honored sir, to engage you in polite conversation? For although your appearance might not command respect, my experience tells me that you are an educated man, not accustomed to drinking. I have always respected education when combined with genuine feeling, and I am, moreover, a titular counselor by rank. Marmeladov -- that is my name; titular counselor. I take the liberty of asking -- have you been in government service?"

"No, I'm a student," the young man answered, somewhat surprised by the man's pompous style and by being addressed so directly. Despite the momentary desire for company he had just been feeling, the instant someone actually spoke to him, he felt his usual irritable, uneasy aversion to any stranger who approached him or tried to.

"A student then, or a former student!" the clerk exclaimed. "Just as I thought! I'm a man of experience, sir, vast experience." He tapped his forehead approvingly. "You've been a student or attended some institute of learning!... But allow me...." He got up, staggered, grabbed his jug and glass, and sat down beside the young man, facing him at a slight angle. He was drunk, but spoke fluently and boldly, only occasionally losing his thread and slurring his words. He latched onto Raskolnikov with the hunger of a man who hadn't spoken to a soul in a month.

"Honored sir," he began with almost ceremonial gravity, "poverty is not a sin -- that's a well-known truth. And I know too that drunkenness is no virtue -- that's even more true. But destitution, honored sir, destitution is a sin. In poverty you can still preserve the nobility of your innate feelings, but in destitution -- never. In destitution, a man isn't driven out of human society with a stick -- he's swept out with a broom, to make it as humiliating as possible. And rightly so! Because in destitution I am the first to degrade myself. Hence the tavern! Honored sir, a month ago Mr. Lebeziatnikov beat my wife, and my wife is a very different person from me! Do you understand? Allow me to ask you one more question, out of simple curiosity: have you ever spent a night on a hay barge on the Neva?"
"No, I haven't," Raskolnikov answered. "What do you mean?"

"Well, I've just come from one, and it's the fifth night I've slept there...." He filled his glass, drained it, and paused. Bits of hay were clinging to his clothes and stuck in his hair. He clearly had not undressed or washed in at least five days. His hands were especially filthy -- plump, red, with black nails.

His monologue seemed to generate a languid, general interest. The boys behind the counter started snickering. The tavern keeper came down from the upper room apparently just to listen to this "entertaining fellow" and sat down a little distance away, yawning lazily but with dignity. Marmeladov was evidently a regular here, and his weakness for grandiose speeches had probably developed from the habit of constantly striking up conversations with all kinds of strangers in taverns. This habit becomes a necessity for certain drunks, especially those who are kept on a tight leash at home. Among fellow drinkers, they try to justify themselves and even win a little respect.
"Entertaining fellow!" the tavern keeper pronounced. "So why don't you work? Why aren't you at your post, if you're in the service?"

"Why am I not at my post, honored sir?" Marmeladov went on, addressing himself exclusively to Raskolnikov, as though it were he who had asked. "Why am I not at my post? Doesn't my heart ache knowing what a useless worm I am? A month ago, when Mr. Lebeziatnikov beat my wife with his own hands, and I lay there drunk -- didn't I suffer? Excuse me, young man, has it ever happened to you... hmm... well, to beg for a loan when you already know it's hopeless?"
"Yes, it has. But what do you mean by hopeless?"

"Hopeless in the fullest sense -- when you know in advance you'll get nothing. You know with absolute certainty that this particular man, this most respectable and upstanding citizen, will under no circumstances give you money. And why should he? He knows I won't pay it back. Out of compassion? But Mr. Lebeziatnikov, who follows all the latest ideas, explained the other day that compassion has been forbidden by science itself, and that's already the practice in England, where they have political economy. Why, I ask you, should he give it to me? And yet, knowing perfectly well that he won't, I set off to see him and..."
"Why do you go?" Raskolnikov asked.

"Well, when you have nobody, when there's nowhere else to go! Every person needs somewhere to go. There are times when you absolutely must go somewhere! When my own daughter first went out with a yellow ticket, I had to go too... (for my daughter holds a yellow passport," he added parenthetically, glancing at the young man with a certain unease.) "Never mind, sir, never mind!" he continued hurriedly and with forced composure when both counter boys burst out laughing and even the tavern keeper smirked. "Never mind, I'm not embarrassed by their mocking! Everyone already knows everything, and all that is hidden shall be revealed. I accept it, not with contempt but with humility. So be it! So be it! 'Behold the man!' Tell me, young man -- no, let me put it more strongly and precisely: not _can_ you, but _dare_ you, looking at me now, say that I am not a pig?"
The young man said nothing.

"Well," the orator resumed stolidly, with even greater dignity, once the laughter in the room had died down. "Well, so be it. I am a pig, but she is a lady! I have the appearance of a beast, but Katerina Ivanovna, my wife, is an educated woman, an officer's daughter. Granted, I am a scoundrel, but she is a woman of noble heart, full of refinement, elevated by her upbringing. And yet... oh, if only she could feel something for me! Honored sir, you see, every person needs at least one place where someone cares about him! But Katerina Ivanovna, though she is generous, she is unjust.... And yet, even though I know that when she pulls my hair it's only out of pity -- for I say it again without shame, she pulls my hair, young man," he declared with renewed dignity, hearing the snickering again, "but God, if she would just once.... But no, no! It's all useless, and there's no point talking! No point! Because more than once my wish did come true, and more than once she did feel sorry for me, but... that is my fate, and I am a beast by nature!"
"You can say that again!" the tavern keeper agreed with a yawn. Marmeladov pounded his fist on the table.

"That is my fate! Do you know, sir, do you know -- I sold her very stockings for drink? Not her shoes, mind you -- that would at least be within the normal order of things -- but her stockings, I sold them for drink! And her mohair shawl too, a gift she'd had for ages, her own property, not mine. And we live in a freezing room, and she caught cold this winter and has started coughing up blood. We have three small children, and Katerina Ivanovna works from morning to night -- scrubbing, cleaning, washing the children -- she was raised to value cleanliness from childhood. But her lungs are weak, she's showing signs of consumption, and I feel it! You think I don't feel it? The more I drink, the more I feel it. That's why I drink -- to find some sympathy and feeling in drink.... I drink so I can suffer twice as much!" And in despair he dropped his head onto the table.

"Young man," he continued, raising his head, "I seem to read some kind of trouble in your face. I noticed it the moment you walked in, and that's why I spoke to you. Because in sharing the story of my life, I don't want to make myself a laughingstock before these idle listeners who know it all already -- I'm looking for a person of feeling and education. Know then that my wife was educated at a prestigious school for noble girls, and upon graduating she performed the shawl dance before the governor and other dignitaries, for which she received a gold medal and a certificate of merit. The medal... well, the medal was sold long ago, hmm... but the certificate is still in her trunk, and not long ago she showed it to our landlady. Even though she's almost always fighting with the landlady, she wanted someone to know about her past honors and happier days. I don't blame her for it, not at all, because the only thing she has left is memories -- everything else has turned to dust and ashes. Yes, yes, she's a proud woman, spirited and determined. She scrubs floors herself and eats nothing but black bread, but she will not tolerate disrespect. That's why she wouldn't stand for Mr. Lebeziatnikov's rudeness, and when he beat her for it, she took to her bed more from the wound to her pride than from the blows. She was a widow when I married her, with three children, each smaller than the last. She had married her first husband, an infantry officer, for love and eloped with him from her father's house. She adored her husband, but he took to cards, got into trouble, and died. He beat her near the end -- though she gave as good as she got, as I have documented proof -- and to this day she speaks of him through tears and throws him in my face. And I'm glad, I'm glad that even if only in her imagination, she can think of herself as having once been happy.... She was left with three children in a remote, godforsaken district where I happened to be at the time, and in such hopeless poverty that, though I've seen my share of hardship, I can't begin to describe it. Her relatives had all abandoned her. And she was proud, fiercely proud.... And then, honored sir, I, a widower at the time with a fourteen-year-old daughter from my first marriage, offered her my hand, because I couldn't bear to see such suffering. You can judge the depth of her desperation -- that she, an educated, cultured woman from a distinguished family, agreed to marry me. But she did! Weeping and wringing her hands, she married me! Because she had absolutely nowhere to turn. Do you understand, sir, do you understand what it means to have absolutely nowhere to turn? No, you don't understand that yet.... For a whole year I did my duty faithfully and never touched this" -- he tapped the jug with his finger -- "because I have feelings. But even so, I couldn't please her. And then I lost my position too, through no fault of my own but due to staff changes, and that's when I did touch it!... It will be a year and a half now since we finally landed in this magnificent capital, adorned with countless monuments, after many wanderings and disasters. Here I found a position.... I found it and lost it again. Do you follow? This time it was my own fault -- my weakness got the better of me.... We now rent part of a room from Amalia Fyodorovna Lippewechsel, and what we live on and how we pay our rent, I couldn't tell you. There are many other people living there besides us. It's chaos, absolute bedlam... hmm... yes... And meanwhile my daughter from my first marriage has grown up. What she had to endure from her stepmother while growing up, I won't speak of. Katerina Ivanovna may be full of generous feelings, but she's a spirited woman, irritable and short-tempered.... But there's no use going into that! Sonya, as you can imagine, received no education. I tried four years ago to teach her some geography and world history, but since I wasn't exactly an expert myself and we had no proper textbooks -- and whatever books we had... hmm, well, we don't even have those now -- so all her education came to an end. We stopped at Cyrus of Persia. Since she's come of age, she's read some romantic novels, and recently she read a book she got through Mr. Lebeziatnikov -- Lewes's Physiology -- have you heard of it? -- and even told us about parts of it. That's the entirety of her education. And now, honored sir, I'd like to ask you a private question. How much do you think a decent, impoverished girl can earn through honest work? She can't make fifteen kopecks a day if she's respectable and has no special talent, not even working without pause! And on top of that, Ivan Ivanovich Klopstock, the civil counselor -- have you heard of him? -- still hasn't paid her for the half-dozen linen shirts she made him, and drove her away with shouting and insults, claiming the collars weren't sewn right and were crooked. And the little ones are going hungry.... And Katerina Ivanovna paces the room wringing her hands, with her cheeks flushed red the way they always are with that disease. 'Here you are living with us,' she says, 'eating and drinking and staying warm, and what do you contribute?' As if there's much to eat and drink when the children haven't seen a crust in three days! I was lying there at the time... well, so what! I was lying there drunk, and I heard my Sonya answer -- she has a gentle spirit, a soft little voice... fair hair, such a pale, thin little face -- she said: 'Katerina Ivanovna, am I really supposed to do something like that?' Now, Darya Frantsovna, a woman of evil reputation well known to the police, had tried two or three times to get to Sonya through the landlady. 'And why not?' Katerina Ivanovna sneered. 'What are you, some kind of treasure that needs protecting?' But don't blame her, don't blame her, honored sir! She wasn't herself when she said it -- she was out of her mind with illness and the children crying from hunger. And she said it more to wound than anything else.... That's Katerina Ivanovna's nature -- when children cry, even from hunger, she starts hitting them. At six o'clock I watched Sonya get up, put on her headscarf and her cape, and leave the apartment. Around nine she came back. She walked straight up to Katerina Ivanovna and laid thirty rubles on the table in front of her, in silence. Not a word, not even a glance -- she just picked up our big green _drap de dames_ shawl, covered her head and face with it, and lay down on the bed facing the wall. Only her small shoulders and body kept shuddering.... And I lay there, same as before.... And then I saw, young man, I saw Katerina Ivanovna, in the same silence, go over to Sonya's little bed. She knelt there all evening, kissing Sonya's feet, and would not get up. And then they both fell asleep in each other's arms... together... yes... and I... lay there drunk."
Marmeladov broke off, as though his voice had given out. Then he hurriedly filled his glass, drank it down, and cleared his throat.

"Since then, sir," he continued after a brief pause, "since then, owing to an unfortunate incident and information supplied by malicious people -- in which Darya Frantsovna played a leading role, claiming she had been treated disrespectfully -- since then my daughter Sofya Semyonovna has been required to carry a yellow ticket, and because of that she can no longer live with us. Our landlady, Amalia Fyodorovna, wouldn't allow it -- though she herself had been in league with Darya Frantsovna before -- and Mr. Lebeziatnikov too... hmm.... All the trouble between him and Katerina Ivanovna was because of Sonya. At first he had tried to court Sonya himself, but then suddenly got on his high horse: 'How,' he said, 'can a man of my education live under the same roof as a girl like that?' And Katerina Ivanovna stood up for her, wouldn't let it go... and that's how things ended up. Sonya visits us now, mostly after dark. She comforts Katerina Ivanovna and gives her everything she can.... She has a room at the Kapernaumovs' -- they're tailors. Kapernaumov is a lame man with a cleft palate, and his entire large family has cleft palates too. His wife as well. They all live in one room, but Sonya has her own, partitioned off.... Hmm... yes... very poor people, all with cleft palates... yes. So I got up the next morning, put on my rags, raised my hands to heaven, and went to see his excellency Ivan Afanasyevich. Do you know his excellency Ivan Afanasyevich? No? Then you don't know a man of God. He is wax... wax before the face of the Lord, even as wax melts!... His eyes were moist when he heard my story. 'Marmeladov, once already you have disappointed my expectations... I'll take you back one more time, on my own responsibility,' he said. 'Remember that,' he said. 'Now you may go.' I kissed the dust at his feet -- in my thoughts only, because in reality he would never have allowed it, being a statesman and a man of modern, progressive, enlightened views. I went home, and when I announced that I'd been taken back into service and would be receiving a salary again -- my God, what a celebration there was!..."

Marmeladov paused again, overwhelmed with emotion. Just then a whole group of revelers, already drunk, came in from the street, and the sound of a hired accordion and the cracked piping voice of a seven-year-old singing "The Village" drifted in from the entrance. The room filled with noise. The tavern keeper and boys busied themselves with the newcomers. Marmeladov, paying no attention to the arrivals, continued his story. He seemed extremely weak by now, but the drunker he got, the more talkative he became. The memory of his recent success in getting the job seemed to revive him, and it actually showed as a kind of glow on his face. Raskolnikov listened closely.

"That was five weeks ago, sir. Yes.... As soon as Katerina Ivanovna and Sonya heard the news -- Lord have mercy, it was as if I'd entered the kingdom of heaven. Before, I could lie around like an animal and get nothing but abuse. Now they were tiptoeing around, shushing the children: 'Semyon Zakharovich is tired from his work at the office, he's resting -- shh!' They made me coffee before work and heated real cream for me! Real cream, do you hear? And how they scraped together the money for a decent set of clothes -- eleven rubles and fifty kopecks -- I can't imagine. Boots, cotton shirt fronts, a uniform -- magnificent, all of it, for eleven and a half rubles. The first morning I came home from the office, Katerina Ivanovna had cooked a two-course dinner: soup and salted beef with horseradish. We'd never dreamed of anything like it. She didn't own any dresses, not a single one, but she made herself up as if she were going visiting -- and with nothing to work with, she managed to look quite presentable. She'd done her hair nicely, put on some kind of clean collar and cuffs, and there she was, a completely different person -- younger, prettier. Sonya, my darling, had only helped with money: 'For the time being,' she said, 'it's better if I don't visit too often. Maybe after dark, when no one can see.' Do you hear that? I lay down for a nap after dinner, and would you believe it -- even though Katerina Ivanovna had quarreled bitterly with our landlady Amalia Fyodorovna just a week before, she couldn't resist inviting her in for coffee. For two hours they sat there whispering. 'Semyon Zakharovich is back in service now, drawing a salary,' she told her, 'and he went to see his excellency in person, and his excellency himself came out to meet him, made everyone else wait, and led Semyon Zakharovich by the hand into his private office.' Do you hear? 'Of course,' he said, 'Semyon Zakharovich, remembering your past services,' he said, 'and despite your unfortunate weakness, since you now give your word and since we've managed poorly without you' -- do you hear? -- 'I am relying on your word as a gentleman.' And all of that, let me tell you, she made up herself, and not just to show off -- no, she actually believes it, she entertains herself with her own fantasies, I swear she does! And I don't blame her, I don't!... Six days ago, when I brought home my first full paycheck -- twenty-three rubles and forty kopecks -- she called me her darling. 'Darling,' she said, 'my little darling.' And when we were alone, you understand? You wouldn't exactly call me a handsome man, and I'm hardly an ideal husband, would you?... Well, she pinched my cheek and said, 'My little darling.'"

Marmeladov broke off. He tried to smile, but his chin suddenly began to tremble. He managed to control himself. The tavern, the degraded appearance of the man, five nights on a hay barge, a jug of spirits, and yet this piercing love for his wife and children -- it left the listener bewildered. Raskolnikov was listening intently but with a feeling of nausea. He regretted having come in here.

"Honored sir, honored sir!" Marmeladov cried, pulling himself together. "Oh, sir, perhaps all this seems laughable to you, as it does to everyone else, and perhaps I'm just annoying you with the stupid details of my wretched home life. But to me it is no laughing matter. Because I feel it all.... And that whole heavenly day, that whole evening, I spent in blissful dreams -- of how I would arrange everything, dress all the children properly, give her some peace, and rescue my own daughter from dishonor and bring her back to her family.... And much more besides.... Perfectly understandable, sir. Well then, sir" -- Marmeladov suddenly gave a sort of jolt, raised his head, and stared intently at his listener -- "well, on the very next day after all those dreams, exactly five days ago, in the evening, through a cunning trick, like a thief in the night, I stole the key to Katerina Ivanovna's box, took out whatever was left of my pay -- how much exactly I've forgotten -- and now look at me, all of you! It's the fifth day since I left home. They're looking for me there, and my job is finished, and my uniform is lying in a tavern by the Egyptian Bridge -- I traded it for these clothes I'm wearing... and it's the end of everything!"

Marmeladov struck his forehead with his fist, clenched his teeth, shut his eyes, and leaned heavily on the table. But a minute later his expression suddenly changed, and with a certain practiced slyness and show of bravado, he looked at Raskolnikov, laughed, and said:
"This morning I went to see Sonya -- went to ask her for some hair of the dog! Ha ha ha!"
"She didn't actually give it to you?" shouted one of the newcomers, then burst into a roar of laughter.

"This very bottle was bought with her money," Marmeladov declared, still addressing only Raskolnikov. "Thirty kopecks she gave me from her own hand, her last kopecks, everything she had -- I could see it.... She said nothing, just looked at me without a word.... That's not something that happens on earth, but up there... up there they grieve over people, they weep, but they don't blame. They don't blame! And that hurts more, it hurts more when they don't blame! Thirty kopecks, yes! And she probably needs them herself now, don't you think? She has to keep up appearances, after all. It costs money, that kind of smartness -- that special kind, you know? Do you understand? She needs pomade, too, petticoats, starched ones, fancy little shoes to show off her foot when she steps over a puddle. Do you understand, sir, do you understand what all that smartness costs? And here I am, her own father, and I took thirty kopecks of that money for a drink! And I'm drinking it! And I've already drunk it! So who's going to feel sorry for a man like me, eh? Do you feel sorry for me, sir, or not? Tell me! Do you feel sorry or not? Ha ha ha!"
He tried to fill his glass, but there was nothing left. The jug was empty.
"What is there to feel sorry about?" the tavern keeper shouted from nearby.

Laughter and curses followed. The laughter and curses came from those who had been listening and also from those who hadn't heard a word but were simply looking at the spectacle of the fired government clerk.
"Feel sorry? Why should anyone feel sorry for me?" Marmeladov suddenly declaimed, rising to his feet with his arm outstretched, as if he had been waiting for exactly that question.

"Why feel sorry for me, you ask? Yes! There's nothing to feel sorry about! I should be crucified, crucified on a cross, not pitied! Crucify me, judge, crucify me -- but pity me while you do it! And then I'll go to be crucified of my own free will, because it's not pleasure I'm after but tears and suffering!... Do you think, you who sell drink, that this bottle has been sweet to me? It was suffering I sought at the bottom of it, tears and suffering, and I found them, I tasted them. But He will have pity on us -- He who had pity on all mankind, who understood every person and everything. He is the One, He is the judge. He will come on that day and He will ask: 'Where is the daughter who sacrificed herself for her sick, consumptive stepmother and for the small children of another? Where is the daughter who had pity on the wretched drunkard, her earthly father, undaunted by his degradation?' And He will say: 'Come to me! I have already forgiven you once.... I have forgiven you once.... Your sins, which are many, are forgiven, for you have loved much....' And He will forgive my Sonya -- He will forgive her, I know it... I felt it in my heart when I was with her just now! And He will judge and forgive everyone -- the good and the wicked, the wise and the humble.... And when He has finished with all of them, He will call out to us: 'You, too, come forward!' He will say. 'Come forward, you drunkards! Come forward, you weaklings! Come forward, you children of shame!' And we will all come forward, without shame, and we will stand before Him. And He will say: 'You are swine, made in the image of the Beast and bearing his mark. But come, even you!' And the wise ones and the clever ones will say: 'Lord, why do you receive these people?' And He will say: 'I receive them, oh wise ones, I receive them, oh clever ones, because not one of them ever believed himself worthy of this.' And He will stretch out His hands to us, and we will fall down before Him... and we will weep... and we will understand everything! Then we will understand everything!... And everyone will understand -- Katerina Ivanovna, too... she will understand.... Lord, Thy kingdom come!" And he collapsed onto the bench, exhausted and helpless, looking at no one, lost in deep thought. His words had made a certain impression. There was a moment of silence, but then the laughter and cursing started up again.
"That's what he thinks!"
"Talked himself into a stupor!"
"Fine government clerk!"
And so on.
"Let's go, sir," Marmeladov said suddenly, raising his head to address Raskolnikov. "Come with me... Kozel's house, through the courtyard. Time I went home to Katerina Ivanovna."

Raskolnikov had been wanting to leave for some time and had already planned to help him. Marmeladov was far unsteadier on his feet than in his speech and leaned heavily on the young man. It was only two or three hundred steps. The closer they got to the house, the more the drunk man was overtaken by fear and confusion.

"It's not Katerina Ivanovna I'm afraid of now," he muttered anxiously, "and not that she'll start pulling my hair. Who cares about my hair! Forget my hair! That's what I say! It's actually better if she does pull it -- that's not what scares me... it's her eyes I'm afraid of... yes, her eyes... the redness in her cheeks frightens me too... and the way she breathes.... Have you noticed how people with that disease breathe when they're worked up? I'm scared of the children crying, too.... Because if Sonya hasn't brought them food... I don't know what's happened! I don't know! But the blows I'm not afraid of.... Know this, sir: those blows are not painful to me -- they're actually a pleasure. I can't do without them, in fact.... It's better this way. Let her hit me -- it eases her heart... it's better.... There's the building. Kozel's building, the cabinetmaker's. A German, well-off. Lead the way!"

They entered through the courtyard and climbed to the fourth floor. The staircase grew darker as they went up. It was nearly eleven o'clock, and though in summer there is no true night in Petersburg, it was very dark at the top of the stairs.

A grimy little door at the very top of the staircase stood ajar. A feeble candle stub lit up a very poor room about ten paces long, all of it visible from the doorway. Everything was in disarray, littered with rags of every kind, mostly children's clothes. A tattered sheet was strung across the far corner -- behind it was probably the bed. The room contained nothing but two chairs and a sofa upholstered in American leather, full of holes, in front of which stood a plain, unpainted, uncovered kitchen table. A sputtering tallow candle in an iron holder stood on the edge of the table. The family apparently had a room to themselves rather than a partitioned space, but their room was essentially a hallway. The door to the other rooms -- or rather the closet-sized compartments into which Amalia Lippewechsel's apartment was divided -- stood half open, and from behind it came shouting, uproar, and laughter. People were apparently playing cards and drinking tea. Profanities of the coarsest kind flew out periodically.

Raskolnikov recognized Katerina Ivanovna at once. She was a fairly tall, slim, graceful woman, terrifyingly thin, with magnificent dark brown hair and a hectic flush on her cheeks. She was pacing back and forth in her tiny room, pressing her hands to her chest; her lips were cracked, her breathing came in ragged, broken gasps. Her eyes burned feverishly and darted around with a harsh, unblinking stare. The consumptive, feverish face, flickering in the last light of the dying candle, made a sickening impression. She looked to Raskolnikov like she was about thirty -- certainly a strange wife for Marmeladov.... She hadn't heard them or noticed them come in. She seemed lost in thought, seeing and hearing nothing. The room was stuffy, but the window was not open; a stench rose from the staircase, but the door to the stairs was not shut. Clouds of tobacco smoke drifted in from the inner rooms. She kept coughing but did not close the door. The youngest child, a girl of about six, was asleep on the floor, curled up with her head on the sofa. A boy a year older stood trembling and crying in the corner -- he had obviously just been beaten. Beside him stood a nine-year-old girl, tall and thin, wearing a threadbare shift and an ancient cashmere shawl draped over her bare shoulders, long outgrown and barely reaching her knees. Her arm, thin as a stick, was wrapped around her brother's neck. She was whispering to him, trying to calm him down, doing everything she could to stop him from whimpering. At the same time, her large dark eyes -- made even larger by the thinness of her terrified face -- were watching her mother with dread. Marmeladov did not step through the door but dropped to his knees right there in the doorway, pushing Raskolnikov ahead of him. The woman, noticing a stranger, paused and faced him with an indifferent stare, coming to her senses for a moment and apparently trying to figure out what he was doing here. She seemed to decide he was heading for the rooms beyond, since he had to pass through hers to get there. Having dismissed him, she walked toward the front door to close it -- and let out a sudden scream when she saw her husband on his knees in the doorway.

"Ah!" she screamed in a frenzy. "He's back! The criminal! The monster!... And where is the money? What's in your pocket? Show me! And your clothes are different! Where are your clothes? Where is the money? Speak!"
She threw herself at him and started searching his pockets. Marmeladov submissively raised both arms to make the search easier. There was not a single kopeck.

"Where is the money?" she shrieked. "Oh, God -- has he drunk it all? There were twelve silver rubles left in the chest!" In a fury she grabbed him by the hair and dragged him into the room. Marmeladov aided her efforts by obediently crawling on his knees.

"And this is a comfort to me! This doesn't hurt at all, it's a genuine com-fort, ho-nored sir!" he called out, his head jerking back and forth in her grip, his forehead even striking the floor once. The child sleeping on the floor woke up and started crying. The boy in the corner lost all control, trembling and screaming, and rushed to his sister in sheer terror, nearly having a fit. The oldest girl stood shaking like a leaf.

"He's drunk it! He's drunk it all!" the poor woman wailed in despair. "And his clothes are gone! And they're hungry, they're hungry!" She wrung her hands and pointed at the children. "Oh, this cursed life! And you -- aren't you ashamed?" She suddenly rounded on Raskolnikov. "From the tavern! You've been drinking with him! You've been drinking with him too! Get out!"

The young man hurried toward the door without a word. The inner door had swung wide open, and curious faces were peering through it. Coarse, laughing faces with pipes and cigarettes, heads wearing caps, crowded the doorway. Further back you could see figures in open dressing gowns and various states of undress, some holding cards. They were especially entertained when Marmeladov, being dragged around by his hair, shouted that it was a comfort to him. Some even started filing into the room. Finally a harsh, shrill screech rang out -- it was Amalia Lippewechsel herself, pushing her way through the crowd, trying to restore order in her own fashion, threatening the poor woman for the hundredth time with eviction the next day. As he left, Raskolnikov managed to reach into his pocket, grab the copper coins he had gotten as change for his ruble in the tavern, and set them on the windowsill unnoticed. Then, on the stairs, he changed his mind and nearly went back.

"What a stupid thing I've done," he thought. "They have Sonya, and I need the money myself." But realizing it would be impossible to take it back now, and that he wouldn't have taken it back anyway, he shrugged it off and headed to his lodgings. "Sonya needs pomade too," he said as he walked, laughing bitterly. "This kind of smartness costs money.... Hmm! And maybe Sonya herself will go bankrupt today, because there's always a risk in it -- hunting big game, panning for gold.... Then they'd all be without a crust tomorrow if it weren't for my money. Good for Sonya! What a gold mine they've dug there! And they're certainly making the most of it! Oh yes, they are! They've cried about it and gotten used to it. People get used to anything, the scoundrels!"
He fell into thought.

"And what if I'm wrong?" he suddenly cried after a moment's reflection. "What if people aren't really scoundrels -- people in general, the whole human race? Then all the rest is just prejudice, invented fears, and there are no real barriers, and everything is exactly as it should be."
